entries.topic: Diocletian's persecution, Constantine's rise, Milvian Bridge accounts, Edict of Milan, deathbed baptism, motive debate

claims.text: On 23 February 303 (the Terminalia) the church at Nicomedia was razed; Lactantius: 'the books of the Holy Scriptures were found, and they were committed to the flames'; the first edict, published next day, ordered destruction of scriptures, liturgical books and places of worship and stripped Christians of rights

Second edict (summer 303) ordered arrest of bishops and priests; fourth edict (304) required universal sacrifice on pain of death; traditores who handed over scriptures were the root of the Donatist schism
Keith Hopkins's tentative estimate: about 6 million Christians c.300, roughly 10% of the empire's population
Galerius's edict (311, Serdica) allowed Christians 'again to be Christians' and to re-establish their places of assembly, asking them to pray for the emperor
Constantius died at York 25 July 306 and Constantine was proclaimed augustus by his army there; Eusebius VC I.22 says the crowd hailed him

Battle of the Milvian Bridge 28 October 312; Lactantius (DMP 44, c.315) reports a dream directing Constantine to mark 'the heavenly sign' on his soldiers' shields, described as a Ch with a line through it; Maxentius was driven into the Tiber

Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History account mentions no vision; his Life of Constantine (after 337) reports a cross of light above the sun about noon with the words 'Conquer by this', seen by the army, told to Eusebius by the emperor 'confirmed by an oath', then a dream of Christ, and describes the labarum with the Chi-Rho
Scholars differ: Norwich doubts the sky vision occurred; Peter Weiss proposed a solar halo; coins with Sol were minted after 312

Arch of Constantine dedicated by the Senate 25 July 315 for his decennalia; inscription credits victory 'instinctu divinitatis' (by the prompting of the divinity) without naming which; no Christian symbolism

Milan letter (Constantine and Licinius), posted 13 June 313: 'the Christians and all others should have liberty to follow that mode of religion which to each of them appeared best'; confiscated places of assembly to be restored 'without money demanded', buyers compensated from the imperial treasury
Constantine died 22 May 337 near Nicomedia; baptised on his deathbed by Eusebius of Nicomedia, an Arian-leaning bishop
Eusebius VC IV.61-64: he had hoped to be baptised in the Jordan; was baptised by 'the prelates' (not named) and refused the purple thereafter, wearing white; died at Pentecost
Crispus executed 326 at Pola; Fausta killed in an overheated bath in 326

Scholarly views on his conversion: Burckhardt essentially unreligious; Peter Brown 'a very Roman conversion'; Leithart sincere 'if a somewhat simple believer'; Drake: favoured Christianity but policy aimed at civic unity
Constantine destroyed a few temples after 324, plundered more (Libanius) to fund Constantinople; an early edict let polytheists keep their rites

entries.topic: Sol Invictus coinage, Sunday law 321, December 25 theories, Mithras parallels, Pontifex Maximus title

claims.text: Aurelian revived the cult of Sol in 274, created a college of pontifices of Sol and built a temple; a dedication on 25 December 274 is reported but Hijmans argues the earliest certain evidence for a 25 December Sol festival is from Julian
Sol continued on Constantine's official coinage until 325/326 (Halsberghe: 323); Sol replaced Mars on his coins from 310
Law of 7 March 321: 'On the venerable day of the Sun let the magistrates and people residing in cities rest'; agricultural work exempt
Eusebius VC IV.18 presents the same rule as enjoining observance of 'the Lord's day, as a day of rest' and records Sunday prayers for soldiers

Justin (c.155): 'on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together'; the well-off 'give what each thinks fit' to support orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners; reason: first day of creation and the resurrection

Earliest Christian record of 25 December as Christ's birth: mid-4th-c. Philocalian calendar; two theories: history-of-religions (borrowed from Sol festival) vs calculation (25 March conception/death, Tertullian c.200); first explicit borrowing claim is a marginal note on Dionysius bar-Salibi (d.1171); McGowan: 'we cannot be entirely sure'
Mosaic c.300 in the Tomb of the Julii (Vatican necropolis) generally read as Christ as Sol/Helios; Hijmans suggests it may simply depict Sol

Mithras is shown emerging from a rock; a 25 December birthday of Mithras is a modern scholarly proposal (Vermaseren), rejected by Beck, while Clauss treats Natalis Invicti as a general Sun festival; zodiac signs appear around tauroctony scenes; cult flourished 1st-4th c. and was eliminated by end of 4th c.
Justin (c.145-155) said 'wicked devils have imitated' the Eucharist in Mithraic rites with bread and a cup of water; Tertullian described a Mithraic bath and forehead mark as a counterfeit of baptism

Every emperor from Augustus to Valentinian I held pontifex maximus; Christian emperors tolerated it; Zosimus IV.36, the only source, says Gratian refused the robe as improper for a Christian; Cameron shows Gratian still bore 'pontifex' in January 379, so repudiation came later

Wikipedia gives 376 or more probably 383 for Gratian's drop; Theodosius used 'pontifex inclytus'; Tertullian c.220 sarcastically called a bishop 'pontifex maximus'; summus pontifex used of bishops generally for centuries
Popes adopted pontifex maximus as a regular honorific in the 15th century (Renaissance); Paul II (1464-71) portrayed as 'Pont. Max.'; it is not among the official titles in the Annuario Pontificio

entries.topic: Clergy privileges, bishops' courts, church building, edict against heretics, Theodosius, book burning by law

claims.text: Constantine to Anullinus (313): clergy to be 'entirely exempted from all public duties' so they are not 'drawn away from the service due to the Deity'
Constantine legislated bishops into judicial roles in 318 and 333, after deciding Donatist appeals with bishop-judges (316); litigants could move cases to a bishop's court
Constantine granted clergy privileges incl. tax exemptions; Lateran basilica built on the Horse Guard base (from 312); Old St Peter's; Holy Sepulchre
VC III.25-43: Constantine ordered the shrine of Venus over the tomb site demolished and a church built at imperial expense; churches at Bethlehem and the Mount of Olives dedicated by Helena
After 320 Constantine endowed the church with land and wealth

VC III.64: edict addressed to 'Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulians, ye who are called Cataphrygians'; III.65: 'none of you henceforth presume to assemble' in public or 'any private house'; their meeting houses 'made over without delay to the catholic Church'; III.66: the law 'directed that search should be made for their books' and many returned to the church
VC IV.36: Constantine ordered from Eusebius fifty copies of the Scriptures on prepared parchment for the churches of Constantinople
Constantine's letter (Socrates I.9): any treatise by Arius found is to be 'consigned to the flames'; concealing one is punished by death
Diocletian and Maximian to Julianus, proconsul of Africa (297 or 302, given at Alexandria 31 March): Manichaean leaders to be burned with their writings; followers' goods confiscated

Edict of Thessalonica (Cunctos populos), 27 February 380, Theodosius with Gratian and Valentinian II (CTh 16.1.2): faith of Peter as professed by Damasus and Peter of Alexandria; others heretics, may not call assemblies churches, punished first by divine then imperial authority; followed by Council of Constantinople 381

Constantius II banned sacrifice in Italy 341 and made sacrifice capital 356 (no evidence of executions); Julian 361-363 restored temples; Gratian 382 diverted subsidies of pagan priests and Vestals, refused pontifex maximus, removed the Altar of Victory

CTh 16.10.10 (391): 'no one is to go to the sanctuaries, walk through the temples'; 16.10.11 closed temples; 16.10.12 (392) banned all pagan sacrifice and worship incl. honouring Lares with fire, Genius with wine, Penates with incense; historians (Errington, Hebblewhite) question their practical effect
Archaeology: only four temple destructions confirmed out of 43 in written sources (Lavan and Mulryan)
CTh 16.5.34 (4 March 398): heretical (Eunomian, Montanist) books to be destroyed, concealment punishable by death; CTh 16.5.66 (3 August 435): Nestorius's books to be burned
